items.explanation: あ is the hiragana for the vowel 'a', said like the 'a' in 'father' but short. Japanese vowels are pure: each one keeps the same sound from start to finish, with no glide at the end.
items.mnemonic: The cross at the top is a stick figure standing over the big swirl below. It slips into the whirlpool and shouts 'Ahhh!'
items.culture_note: Hiragana grew out of cursive handwriting of Chinese characters around the 9th century. あ is a simplified cursive form of the kanji 安. Much of the court literature of the Heian period, including The Tale of Genji, was written largely in hiragana.

items.explanation: い is the hiragana for 'i', said like the 'ee' in 'see' but short.
items.mnemonic: Two short strokes side by side, like the letters 'ii' stretched into lines. Read them as 'ee'.
items.culture_note: い comes from a cursive form of the kanji 以. It is also the first kana of the iroha, a classical poem that uses each of the 47 kana of its time exactly once and was long used to put things in order, the way English uses the alphabet.

items.explanation: う is the hiragana for 'u', close to the 'oo' in 'food' but short, and with relaxed lips instead of rounded ones. In some words it is almost whispered: です (desu) often sounds like 'des'.
items.mnemonic: Under the little dash of a hat, the big curve is a letter 'U' tipped onto its side.
items.culture_note: う comes from a cursive form of the kanji 宇.

items.explanation: え is the hiragana for 'e', said like the 'e' in 'bed'.
items.mnemonic: A dancer with a small hat on, kicking one leg out to the side and calling 'Eh!' to the crowd.
items.culture_note: え comes from a cursive form of the kanji 衣.

items.explanation: お is the hiragana for 'o', like the 'o' in 'go' but pure, without the 'w' sound English adds at the end. It looks like あ with an extra stroke on the right, so check for that stroke when you read.
items.mnemonic: お is あ with a small piece flying off to the right: 'Oh! Something fell off!'
items.culture_note: お comes from a cursive form of the kanji 於. The お in おちゃ is a polite prefix: ちゃ alone means tea, and adding お makes the word sound more refined. Many everyday words take this prefix, such as おみず (omizu, water), which is one way politeness is built into ordinary Japanese.
